questions.q: Which statement of the single responsibility principle is most useful when deciding how to split code?
questions.explain: "One thing" is too vague to apply. Asking who requests changes (finance, accounting, customer service) shows where two groups' wishes can collide inside one module.
options: Every class should have exactly one method
Every file should be shorter than 100 lines
A module should answer to one actor: one group of people who ask for its changes
A class should only use one other class

questions.q: A shared money() helper formats amounts for both customer invoices and the accounting CSV export. Finance wants naira signs and commas for customers. What is the SRP-minded fix?
questions.explain: The total is one piece of knowledge and should be shared. How it is displayed belongs to each consumer. A boolean parameter would keep both actors tied to the same function and is control coupling.
options: Add a forCsv boolean parameter to money()
Keep one shared calculation of the total, and give each consumer its own formatting, owned by that consumer
Ask accounting to accept commas in amounts
Copy the whole invoice class for each consumer

questions.q: A team splits invoice totals into SubtotalCalculator, VatCalculator and TotalAdder. Finance changes all three together every time. What went wrong?
questions.explain: The test is who asks for changes, not size. One actor, one reason to change: one module. Splitting it lowers cohesion.
options: Nothing, smaller classes are always better
SRP was read as "one thing per class". The three classes serve one actor and change together, so one responsibility is now scattered
They should have used inheritance
They should add interfaces for each calculator

questions.q: What does "open for extension, closed for modification" mean in practice?
questions.explain: Bug fixes are still made in place. OCP is about the axis that keeps changing: new cases arrive as new objects behind a stable interface.
options: Code may never be edited once it is released
New behaviour on a frequently changing axis can be added as new code (a new promotion object, a new middleware) without editing code that already works
All classes must be declared with extends in mind
Every function must accept a configuration object

questions.q: Which of these most deserves an extension point (a list of pluggable objects) rather than a switch?
questions.explain: Extension points pay off where cases arrive often. Small closed sets that belong to the domain are better as a union with an exhaustive switch.
options: Invoice status: draft, sent, paid
Days of the week
Marketing promotions, which change every few weeks and are requested by people outside the team
HTTP methods GET and POST in a tiny internal tool

questions.q: In an exhaustive switch over "draft" | "sent" | "paid", what does const unhandled: never = status; after the switch do?
questions.explain: After every handled case, the remaining type is never. A new union member leaves a real type there, and assigning it to never fails. The compiler finds every switch that needs updating.
options: It throws at run time when a case is missing
If someone adds a new member such as "void" to the union and forgets a case, the assignment becomes a compile error at that exact spot
It makes the function return never
It turns off type checking for the switch

questions.q: InvoiceStore.find(number) is documented to return undefined for an unknown number. Which implementation breaks the Liskov substitution principle?
questions.explain: Callers written against the interface check for undefined; they do not expect an exception. The implementation promises less than the interface, so code that works with other stores crashes with this one.
options: One that caches results in memory
One that accepts both upper- and lower-case numbers
One that throws "ERR 404" for an unknown number
One that logs every call

questions.q: Both store classes say implements InvoiceStore and compile. Why can one still break LSP?
questions.explain: Types describe shapes. Behavioural promises need tests, which is what a contract test run against every implementation provides.
options: Because implements is ignored in strict mode
Because implements only checks method types, not behaviour such as "returns undefined when not found"
Because TypeScript does not support interfaces at run time
It cannot; compiling proves substitutability

questions.q: What is a contract test?
questions.explain: A contract test is the practical tool for LSP. It also keeps in-memory fakes honest: if the fake passes and the real adapter fails, the fake has been lying to your other tests.
options: A test that checks the legal terms of an API
One test suite written against an interface, run against every implementation (fake and real), so they all keep the same promises
A test that only runs in production
A type check of the interface

questions.q: Which change to an implementation is allowed by LSP?
questions.explain: An implementation may demand less and promise more, never demand more or promise less. Extra requirements break callers that rely on the interface.
options: Only accepting invoice numbers in upper case, while the interface accepts any string
Returning null where the interface promises an invoice or undefined
Accepting a wider range of input than the interface requires, and still returning what it promises
Throwing for inputs the interface allows

questions.q: A test fake for a reminder job has to stub eleven repository methods with throw new Error("not used"). Which principle is this pointing at?
questions.explain: The job should ask for a small interface such as OverdueInvoices with listOverdue. Then its fake is one function, and changes to unrelated repository methods cannot affect it.
options: Liskov substitution
Interface segregation: the job depends on a fat interface instead of the one method it uses
Open/closed
DRY

questions.q: After you define a small OverdueInvoices interface, does the big repository class need implements OverdueInvoices to be passed to the job?
questions.explain: Structural typing makes ISP cheap in TypeScript: the consumer declares what it needs, and existing classes fit automatically. implements is still useful as a check where the class is written.
options: Yes, otherwise TypeScript rejects it
No. TypeScript is structural: any object with a matching listOverdue fits, whether it declares implements or not
Yes, and it must also extend a base class
No, but only if the method is static

questions.q: What is the misapplied form of interface segregation?
questions.explain: Segregate by consumer. An interface should match what one kind of caller needs, often a few methods that belong together.
options: Having a repository class with many methods
Splitting everything into one-method interfaces, so each class implements many tiny interfaces and one idea is scattered
Using Pick to select methods
Writing a fake in tests

questions.q: In dependency inversion, who owns (defines) the ReminderSender interface?
questions.explain: The inversion is in the source dependency: details import the interface that policy defines, so policy never imports details.
options: The SMTP library
The reminder job, the high-level policy that uses it; the SMTP code imports it and implements it
A shared interfaces/ folder that nobody owns
The DI container

questions.q: Which statement correctly separates dependency inversion, dependency injection and a DI container?
questions.explain: You can invert dependencies and inject by hand with no container at all, as the reminder job does. A container only automates the wiring.
options: They are three names for the same thing
Inversion is a rule about which way source dependencies point; injection is passing collaborators in; a container is a tool that does the injection from registrations
Injection is a rule, inversion is a tool, a container is a pattern
A container is required for inversion

questions.q: When is an interface in front of a class with only one real implementation worth it?
questions.explain: A class that calls a bank's API effectively has two implementations: the real one and the test fake. Internal logic with one implementation gets no benefit from an IThing/ThingImpl pair.
options: Always; every class should have an IClass interface
Never; one implementation means no interface
When it crosses a process boundary (network, disk, clock) so tests need a fake, and policy code should not know its details
Only when the class has more than ten methods

questions.q: A function takes rates: ExchangeRates (a class). Tests passed { rate: async () => 0.00065 }. After a #cache field is added to the class, the test no longer compiles. Why?
questions.explain: That is the moment to extract an interface owned by the consumer, such as RateSource. The change is local: callers that pass real instances do not change.
options: Private fields make classes final
A class with a private member only accepts real instances of that class as its type, because no other object can have that private member
The fake's method must now be synchronous
TypeScript forbids object literals as arguments

questions.q: Which is real duplication that DRY asks you to remove?
questions.explain: DRY is about knowledge. If the VAT rate changes, all three copies must change: one fact, three places. The two fees only look alike; they change for different reasons.
options: Two fee functions that are both "2% with a ₦500 minimum" today, owned by different teams
The VAT rate written in the checkout, the invoice and the receipt
Two loops that both iterate over an array
Two tests that both create an order

questions.q: A merged feeKobo(subtotal, kind, options) has grown flags, and a weekend surcharge meant for delivery now also applies to the service fee. What is the best next step?
questions.explain: Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Once a shared function needs kind === … checks, the cases were never the same knowledge. Undo the merge and let each rule evolve on its own.
options: Add another flag to exclude the service fee from the surcharge
Split it back into deliveryFeeKobo and serviceFeeKobo, even though they share a line of code
Move the function into a base class
Make the options global

questions.q: What does the "rule of three" suggest?
questions.explain: Two examples are rarely enough to tell real shared knowledge from coincidence. With three, the common part and the differences are clearer.
options: Every function should have at most three parameters
Tolerate a second copy of similar code; extract a shared abstraction on the third, when you can see what really is shared
Write three tests for every function
Split any class with three methods

questions.q: A configurable discount "rule engine" stores operators as strings like "gte". A rule with "gte " (trailing space) silently never matches. Which principle does this illustrate?
questions.explain: The simplest design that solves the real problem was a five-line function. The engine added moving parts that nobody needed and hid bugs from every tool.
options: Interface segregation
KISS: the clever design turned code into strings, so the compiler and editor can no longer catch mistakes; a plain function would make the typo a compile error
Liskov substitution
Dependency inversion

questions.q: A developer says: "KISS, so I skipped input validation and error handling." What is wrong with this?
questions.explain: The tangled checkout function was easy to write and very hard to change. Simplicity is about the result, not about how little effort went in today.
options: Nothing; less code is simpler
Simple is not the same as easy. A simple design has few moving parts and handles the real cases; leaving out error handling makes the system harder to operate, not simpler
KISS only applies to front-end code
Validation should be done by the database only

questions.q: Which of these should you decide now, even though YAGNI says to avoid speculative work?
questions.explain: YAGNI is about cost of adding later. Money stored as floats cannot be fixed by refactoring: the rounded values are already in the database. The other three can be added when needed.
options: Support for a second payment provider
A plugin system for export formats
Storing money as integer kobo rather than floating-point naira
A caching layer

questions.q: Which pair of principles pulled against each other in the invoice money() helper?
questions.explain: Shared code couples everyone who uses it. When the users are different actors with different wishes, a small duplication can be the better design.
options: KISS and YAGNI
DRY and SRP: sharing the helper removed duplication but tied two actors (customers and accounting) to one piece of code
ISP and LSP
OCP and DIP

questions.q: Which code review comment is most useful?
questions.explain: Principles are vocabulary for explaining a concrete risk, not verdicts. Naming the risk lets the author judge whether the trade-off is worth it.
options: "This violates SRP."
"Use SOLID."
"This helper is used by both the customer invoice and the accounting export, so a format change for customers would break the nightly import."
"Too many lines."

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The thousands separator adds a comma inside the amount, so splitting on commas gives four fields. Formatting meant for people broke a format meant for machines.
options: INV-7,Adaeze Stores,₦14415.75 3
INV-7,Adaeze Stores,₦14,415.75 4
INV-7,Adaeze Stores,₦1,441,575 5
INV-7,Adaeze Stores,₦14,415.75 3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first matching branch wins, so on Saturday the smaller weekend discount hides the first-order discount. The priority is encoded only in the line order.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: At 4000 only the weekend promo applies. At 20000, 10% (2000) beats 500. At 60000, 10% is 6000, which beats the bulk 2500. The policy "best single discount" is explicit, not a matter of order.
options: weekend:500 ten:2000 bulk:2500
weekend:500 ten:2000 ten:6000
none:0 ten:2000 ten:6000
weekend:500 bulk:2500 bulk:2500

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only fields containing a quote, comma or newline are wrapped in quotes, and quotes inside are doubled. That is the CSV rule accounting's importer expects.
options: INV-8,Musa "Big" Stores, Kano,1441575
"INV-8","Musa ""Big"" Stores, Kano","1441575"
INV-8,"Musa ""Big"" Stores, Kano",1441575
INV-8,"Musa "Big" Stores, Kano",1441575

questions.q: A tiny contract check is run against two stores. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both stores satisfy the same type, but the legacy one throws where the contract promises undefined. The shared check finds it; a type check cannot.
options:
memory PASS
legacy PASS

memory PASS
legacy FAIL ERR 404

memory PASS
legacy FAIL

memory FAIL
legacy FAIL ERR 404

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 2% of 1,000,000 is 20,000, so the ₦500 minimum (50,000 kobo) applies, plus the 30,000 surcharge. The surcharge ignores kind, so the service fee rises too: the merged function mixed two rules.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second rule's operator is "GTE", which matches no branch and silently counts as false. Strings hide mistakes that a typed function would turn into compile errors.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Mailer has only public members, so any object with a matching send fits its type. The real class is never called. "Your invoice is overdue" has 23 characters.
options: would contact the SMTP server for musa@shop.ng
musa@shop.ng <- 23 chars
musa@shop.ng <- Your invoice is overdue
A type error: fake is not a Mailer

questions.q: The status comes from a JSON file written by an older program. What does this print?
questions.explain: The as assertion told the compiler something untrue. At run time the value is "void", no case matches, and the fallback line runs. Exhaustiveness checks protect code, not data from outside: validate that at the boundary.
options: Not sent
undefined
unknown status: void
A TypeError is thrown

questions.q: An implementation adds a requirement the interface does not have. What does this print?
questions.explain: The strict store demands more of its callers than the interface does (a stronger precondition), so a caller that works with the flexible store fails with this one. That breaks Liskov substitution.
options:
saved inv-9
saved inv-9

saved inv-9
numbers must be upper case

saved INV-9
saved INV-9

numbers must be upper case
numbers must be upper case

questions.q: Write toAccountingRow(invoice) for the accounting export: the number, the customer and the total in whole kobo, joined by commas. Any field containing a comma or a quote must be wrapped in double quotes with inner quotes doubled. The program should print INV-8,"Musa, Sons & Co",950000.
questions.explain: The export owns its own format: machine-friendly kobo and proper CSV quoting. The customer-facing naira formatting lives elsewhere, so a change there cannot break this.

questions.q: Add a loyalty promotion (₦1,000 off, i.e. 100000 kobo, for customers with orders >= 5) as a new object in the list, without editing bestDiscount. The program should print loyalty 100000 then first 150000.
questions.explain: bestDiscount is closed for modification and open for extension: a new promotion is a new object in the list. Existing promotions and their tests are untouched.

questions.q: Write contract(name, store) that checks two promises of the TaskStore interface and prints PASS name or FAIL name: saving a task then finding it returns the same title, and finding an unknown id returns undefined (an exception counts as FAIL). The program should print PASS memory then FAIL legacy.
questions.explain: The same checks run against every implementation. The legacy store satisfies the type but not the promise, which is exactly the Liskov violation a contract test exists to catch.

questions.q: Change countOverdue so it asks only for what it uses: a parameter of type OverdueSource (an interface with just listOverdue(): string[]). Then call it with a one-method fake returning ["INV-3", "INV-5"]. The program should print 2.
questions.explain: The function now depends on one method. Any full repository still fits OverdueSource structurally, and the test fake is a single function instead of four stubs.

questions.q: Undo the premature merge: replace feeKobo with two functions, deliveryFeeKobo(subtotal, weekend) (2% with a 50000 minimum, plus 30000 on weekends) and serviceFeeKobo(subtotal) (2% with a 50000 minimum, no surcharge). The program should print 80000 50000.
questions.explain: The two fees share one line of code today but belong to different owners and change for different reasons. As two functions, the weekend rule cannot leak into the service fee.

questions.q: Write statusLabel(status) for "draft" | "sent" | "paid" | "void" with a switch that handles every case (Draft, Sent, Paid, Cancelled) and ends with a never check, so a future member would be a compile error. The program should print Draft Sent Paid Cancelled.
questions.explain: For a small closed set, an exhaustive switch is simpler than a plugin registry, and the never line makes the compiler list every switch to update when the set grows.

questions.q: Replace the string-based rule engine with one plain typed function bigOrderDiscountKobo(subtotalKobo): 100000 off when the subtotal is at least 2000000, otherwise 0. The program should print 100000 0.
questions.explain: One typed line replaces the engine. A misspelled name or operator is now a compile error instead of a promotion that silently never applies.
